items.quote: How the True Physick, which is covered bark and rind, is to be got out, and rightly prepared by Fire.
items.note: The chapter heading announces its subject: how the True Physick is got out and prepared by Fire.

items.quote: which is covered bark and rind
items.note: The heading says the True Physick is covered, with bark and rind as the covering.

items.quote: ALL things in respect of the first matter were created perfect, but the Chymist perfecteth the last matter by Fire
items.note: Things were created perfect as to the first matter; the Chymist perfects the last matter by Fire.

items.quote: The Physitian perfecteth the Creature of God by Fire.
items.note: The margin note names the Physitian as the one who perfects by Fire, where the paragraph beside it names the Chymist.

items.quote: nothing in this lower world (which is subject to generation and corruption) is so noble but hath Poyson in it selfe
items.note: Everything in the lower world, however noble, has Poyson in itself.

items.quote: where there is hurt there is also help, where there is venome there is vertue
items.note: In God's chief works harm and help, venom and virtue stand together.

items.quote: should alwayes be joyned together in all things, to put us dayly in mind of the Fear of God
items.note: Good and evil are joined in all things by Nature's ordering, to remind us daily of the Fear of God.

items.name: Eccl.
items.note: The margin note names Eccl. 39.26 beside the words on Good and Evill joined in all things.

items.quote: As soon as the Omnipotent gave Power to Man, presently he raised up an enemy, least the Power growing lazy should loose its Nature
items.name: Firmianus
items.note: Words the text gives to Firmianus: man was given an enemy together with power, so that the power should not grow lazy.

items.quote: as the Poet said, nothing is in every respect happy
items.name: the Poet
items.note: A saying given to an unnamed Poet; the lines given do not show which poet.

items.quote: Nil ex omni
items.name: the Poet
items.note: A Latin margin note, partly illegible, stands beside the Poet's saying; it names no person.

items.quote: that man partaker of the Divine Nature, and Lord of all living creatures, should be vexed with Ghosts, and hurryed with Furies
items.note: Man, though partaker of the Divine Nature and lord of creatures, is vexed and harried; drawn as a consequence from the two sayings.

items.name: Wisd.; Eccl.
items.note: The margin note names places in Wisd. and Eccl. beside the passage given to Roger Bacon.

items.quote: in the same place or thing where of his MERCY he appoynted plenty of Physick, even there also by the power of his incomprehensible Justice he substituted Poyson to guard it
items.name: Roger Bacon
items.note: Given to Roger Bacon the English Phylosopher: where God's Mercy set Physick, his Justice set Poyson to guard it.

items.quote: Thistles and prickles of Roses the inseperable companions and avengers of transgressions
items.note: Thistles and rose prickles are set beside the guarding Poyson as companions and avengers of transgressions; a figure for the poison that goes with the physick.

items.quote: Good cannot be known but by evill, and the Enemy being discovered the danger may be avoyded.
items.note: Good is known only through evil, and a discovered enemy can be avoided. The lines do not show whether this is still Bacon's or the author's own.

items.quote: The severe Justice of God is the disease & venome in all things: on the contrary, the Mercy of God is the Physick in Nature and in all things.
items.note: The margin note says what the Justice and the Mercy of God are in things: Justice the disease and venom, Mercy the Physick.

items.quote: Holy Hermes the most Ancient Divine (together with Ecclesiasticus) writeth in his Key that all sublunary things ought to consist of contraposition and contrariety
items.name: Hermes
items.note: Given to Hermes in a writing called his Key, with Ecclesiasticus named as agreeing: sublunary things consist of contraries.

items.quote: and this after another manner may be of things Impossible in respect of the generation and corruption of things
items.name: Hermes
items.note: A further clause that seems to continue the report of Hermes; its sense is obscure in the wording given and it is not clear whose words they are.

items.quote: All things that are awlesse are also lawlesse
items.note: A saying resting on the English pair awlesse and lawlesse. A margin note in foreign script, not transcribed, stands just before it.

items.quote: nor can Man any other way attaine to the highest pitch unlesse he resolve constantly to maintaine the good fight that is finished in faelicity
items.note: Man reaches the highest pitch only by constantly maintaining the good fight.

items.quote: God by his Wisdome hath ordained that Sympathy and Antipathy should be alike good, by which spectacle of Nature he would stir up mortall men to contemplate and search out his secrets
items.note: Sympathy and Antipathy are ordained as alike good, to stir men to search out God's secrets.

items.quote: to contemplate and search out his secrets
items.note: God is said to have secrets that men are to search out by looking at Nature.

items.quote: that if one man hate another, he that is hated might cover and cure the defect of the malicious
items.note: An application to men: the hated one may cover and cure the defect of the one who hates.

items.quote: Heraclitus called Nature the daughter of War
items.name: Heraclitus
items.note: A name for Nature given to Heraclitus.

items.quote: Homer called it Contention
items.name: Homer
items.note: A name for Nature given to Homer.

items.name: Eccl.
items.note: The margin note names places in Eccl. beside the passage on Sympathy and Antipathy.

items.quote: The cause of Simpathy and Antipathy.
items.what: The cause of Simpathy and Antipathy
items.note: The margin note heads the paragraph as giving the cause of Simpathy and Antipathy.

items.quote: Man is his own enemy; the Cause of dissolution and death in this our Kingdome divided in it selfe, the intestine duell
items.note: Man is his own enemy; the cause of death is an inward division, called a kingdom divided and an intestine duel.

items.quote: in the little world, the body
items.note: The text puts the body beside the little world as its meaning here.

items.quote: in it lyeth hid the preserver and destroyer of health
items.note: The preserver and the destroyer of health are both said to lie hid in the body.

items.quote: the Saints have called the mortall body Hell and Purgatory, wherein continuall war is to be made
items.name: the Saints
items.note: Names for the mortal body given to the Saints.

items.quote: seeing the Anotomy of Death findeth entertainment in the whole State of our Life
items.note: The reason given for the Physitians' office: the Anotomy of Death is present through the whole of life. The lines given do not say what the phrase means.

items.name: Eccl.
items.note: The margin note names Eccl. 38.15 at the end of the sentence on the body as a place of continual war.

items.quote: Nature hath commanded the Physitians to be ministers, and to seperate, not masters to compose
items.note: The Physitian's office is to serve and to separate, not to compose as a master.

items.quote: our Remedies require preparations, separations and exaltations before they can impart their hidden and restrained vertues
items.note: Three kinds of work are named for remedies: preparations, separations, exaltations.

items.quote: their hidden and restrained vertues
items.note: The virtues of remedies are called hidden and restrained until the work is done.

items.quote: As all things are proved by Fire, so also the Tryall of the knowledge of Physick is to be made by Fire
items.note: Knowledge of Physick is to be tried by Fire.

items.quote: Physick and Chymistry cannot be separated
items.note: Physick and Chymistry belong together.

items.quote: Chymistry (not that which Mountebanks use to paint Faces with to make them White and Red)
items.note: The text sets its Chymistry apart from another thing of the same name, the face-painting of Mountebanks.

items.quote: doth make manifest, not onely the true Simples, Wonders, Secrets, Mysteries, Vertues, Forces respecting health
items.note: Chymistry is said to make manifest secrets and mysteries concerning health.

items.quote: the Archaeon Ventricle or Naturall In-bred Chymist
items.note: The Archaeon Ventricle is glossed as the natural in-bred Chymist, which Chymistry imitates.

items.quote: it teacheth to segregate every mystery into into its own reservacle, and to free the medicines from those scurvy raggs wherein they were wrapt up
items.note: Two steps: each mystery is set apart into its own reservacle, and the medicines are freed from what wraps them.

items.quote: a due separation from the impurities and corruptible and filthy mixture of superficiall and externall Elements, that that pure and Christiline matter may be administred to our bodies
items.note: The means is separation from the outward, impure Elements; the result is a pure Christiline matter to be given to the body.

items.quote: But to deliver this from prison and captivity, Hoc opus, hic labor est, is a hard task to performe.
items.note: The pure matter is spoken of as held in prison; freeing it is called a hard task, with a Latin phrase beside the English.

items.quote: without this Chymicall Phylosophy all Physick is but livelesse; Without Alchymicall skill there can be no Speculative or Practick Physick
items.note: Physick without Chymicall Phylosophy is lifeless; both speculative and practick Physick need Alchymicall skill.

items.quote: He that rejecteth that knowledge being disheartned by the difficulty thereof shall never find where the disease lyeth.
items.note: Whoever gives up this knowledge for its difficulty will not find where the disease lies.

items.quote: our common sort of Physitians are not to be followed, who patronize their sloth under other mens paines and study
items.note: The common Physitians are not to be followed; they are charged with sloth.

items.quote: use to leave the preparation of their medicines most commonly to some carelesse and covetous Apothecary to the great dammage of their Patients
items.note: Their fault named: leaving the preparation of medicines to a careless Apothecary.

items.quote: I speake not against the conscientious Apothecaries who by their trusty diligence serve the Common Wealth as the Alchymy of Vulcan
items.note: The author excepts the conscientious Apothecaries and likens their service to the Alchymy of Vulcan; the lines do not explain that name.

items.quote: By this artificall resolution of bodyes the propertyes which before layd in the compositions of them are now brought to light.
items.note: The work is named a resolution of bodies; it brings out the properties that lay in their composition.

items.quote: as by a certaine kinde of artificiall Tynosure, or figures of stars the Chymists have not only made curtaines extending to all the borders of Nature
items.note: A comparison marked as such: the resolution is like an artificiall Tynosure or figures of stars, by which the Chymists made curtaines to Nature's borders. The sense of the figure is not stated.

items.quote: this true Analysis and vitall Anatomy of bodies
items.what: this true Analysis and vitall Anatomy of bodies
items.note: The same work is named a true Analysis and a vitall Anatomy of bodies, in which a Physitian should be exercised.

items.quote: (as hath been said)
items.note: The author says he has said before that the Physitian should be exercised in this Analysis; the place is not named.

items.quote: there is no constant quality of any body which is not to be found either in the Salt, or Mercury, or Sulphur of the same body
items.note: Every constant quality of a body is found in its Salt, Mercury or Sulphur.

items.quote: all compound bodies of the inferiour Globe are to be distributed into three orders or companies; into Animalls, Vegetables, and Mineralls
items.what: three orders or companies; Animalls, Vegetables, and Mineralls
items.note: Compound bodies are first to be sorted into three numbered orders.

items.quote: the individualls of all these, and the parts of the individualls are diligently to be examined
items.note: The step named: examine the individuals of each order and their parts.

items.quote: the three First things (viz. Salt, Sulphur, and Mercury)
items.note: The text says which the three First things are: Salt, Sulphur and Mercury.

items.quote: in the shop of Nature there is Animall, Vegetable, Minerall Salt; Animall, vegetable, minerall Sulphur; vegetable, animall, minerall Mercury
items.note: Each of the three First things is found in each of the three orders, nine in all.

items.quote: Vegetables comprehend plants, trees, Zoophyts.
items.note: The margin note says what the order of Vegetables holds, Zoophyts among them.

items.quote: Animalls are the beasts in their order, creeping swimming, flying, four footed creatures.
items.note: The margin note says what the order of Animalls holds.

items.quote: The first face of Things was pure, sound, perfect without corruption and death
items.note: At first things were pure and without corruption or death.

items.quote: created all things good by his Will, that all things might glorifie him and live holily and incorruptably according to the prescribed order
items.note: God made all things good, to glorify him and live incorruptibly.

items.quote: Man at first was created healthy, (sicknesse entred by the Woman, not by the Man)
items.note: Man was created healthy; sickness is said to have entered by the Woman.

items.quote: there appeared two contraries, the externall corruptable, and the internall compleat, which could not long continue in one without unavoydable corruption
items.note: Death entered because two contraries, an outward corruptible and an inward complete, could not last together in one.

items.quote: after the transgression and fall from unity to alterity, by the curse of God new Tinctures came in (even infinite evills)
items.note: After the fall new Tinctures came in by God's curse; the bracket puts them beside infinite evils.

items.quote: the beauty of the whole Creature was transplanted
items.note: The change in the Creature after the fall is called a transplanting; the margin note N169 says what that is.

items.quote: The transplantation of the Creature is by the calamity and coming in of sicknesse upon it
items.note: The margin note says what the transplantation of the Creature is: the coming in of sickness upon it.

items.quote: which causeth sicknesse and death by in-bred contrariety and corruption
items.note: The margin note: since the Fall an enemy is carried within, causing sickness and death by in-bred contrariety.

items.quote: Impurity was joyned to the pure roots, which was the predestination of diseases.
items.note: Impurity joined to the pure roots is called the predestination of diseases.

items.quote: the roots of sicknesses in certaine individuall or species doe not consist apart by themselves, but are implanted and mixt in the pure and first seeds of things
items.note: The roots of sicknesses do not stand apart; they are mixed in the pure first seeds of things.

items.quote: the foure wombs or Elements
items.note: The four wombs are put beside the Elements as the same; in them the seeds spring up whose fruits are the nourishments.

items.quote: Nature therefore, as it is now, gives us nothing that is pure in the world, but hath mixed all things with many impurities
items.note: Nature as it now is gives nothing pure; all is mixed with impurities.

items.quote: it might often put us in mind that we should begin to learn the knowledge of Chymistry from our cradles
items.note: The impurity is a spur of necessity to learn Chymistry from the cradle.

items.quote: so long as we are shut out of Paradice into the subburbs of this world
items.note: This world is called the suburbs into which we are shut out of Paradice.

items.quote: we ought to till and manure the EARTH, to wit, the whole frame of the world
items.note: The text says what EARTH means here: the whole frame of the world, so tilling is not meant of soil alone.

items.quote: by admiration, searching into, and knowledge of both the Visible and Invisible (Limus) Earth
items.note: The tilling is said to be done by admiration, searching and knowledge; the Earth is twofold, Visible and Invisible, with Limus set in brackets beside it.

items.quote: as Natures Labourers, not lazily, but in the sweat of our browes
items.note: We are to labour for bread and necessaries as Natures Labourers.

items.quote: in this LAND of LABOUR to attain the fruits of Terrene and Caelestiall Wisdome
items.note: The world is named, in capitals, the LAND of LABOUR; the aim of the labour is the fruits of Terrene and Caelestiall Wisdome.

items.quote: by doing nothing we should learn to doe naughtily
items.note: Idleness is feared as the teacher of wrongdoing.

items.quote: And this is the true end of Mans Creation, that in the fear of God and love of his neighbor he should manage the Earth, recovering what he hath lost, and not be idle
items.what: the true end of Mans Creation
items.note: The text announces the true end of man's creation: to manage the Earth, recovering what he lost.

items.quote: the Light of Nature not after his own, but according to the will of his Creator
items.note: Man is to walk in the Light of Nature according to the Creator's will, not his own.

items.quote: he should continue the Instrument, Habitation and Tabernacle of God
items.note: Man is to remain God's instrument, habitation and tabernacle.

items.quote: he should through Nature search out the wonderfull works of God by consideration of Temporall and Caelestiall observations, thereby to make known the invisible works of God
items.note: Man is to search out God's works through Nature and make the invisible works known.

items.quote: his marvellous works, wonders and mysteries which he hath revealed
items.note: God's works are called mysteries and are said to be revealed by him.

items.quote: He that hath learned to know God & himselfe hath ordered the Earth with good husbandry
items.note: The margin note makes knowing God and oneself the same as ordering the Earth with good husbandry, a second sense of the husbandry in the paragraph.

items.quote: idlenesse the pillow & cushion of the Devill is removed by labour and diligence
items.note: The margin note: idleness is removed by labour and diligence.

items.quote: But to passe from Food let us come to Physick
items.note: The author marks a turn of subject from Food to Physick.

items.quote: unlesse he had rather eate the husk and shells with the kernell, as the former and more rugged generations have done
items.note: Refusing the art is likened to eating husk and shells with the kernel, as earlier generations did.

items.quote: this Separatory art which teacheth rightly to discerne and seperate the Good from the Bad, the Profitable from the Unprofitable
items.note: The art is named the Separatory art and said to teach the separating of good from bad; a long row of pairs follows.

items.quote: the minerall Spirit from the Anthos or blossome
items.note: Anthos is glossed as blossome; it stands in the row of things separated, against the minerall Spirit.

items.quote: Poyson from healing Medicines and Balsoms, Light from Darknesse, Life from Death, Day from Night, Visible from Invisible,
items.note: Further pairs the art separates; the order of good and bad within the pairs is not kept the same.

items.quote: that which is pure Celestiall, the kernall and Marrow, from that which is Terrestrial Impure, the Rinds, and Membranes, the Covers, Shells, Husks and dreggs
items.note: The text says what kernel and rinds stand for: the pure Celestiall part against the Terrestrial Impure part.

items.quote: the Coate aed Cottage of Physick which are enemyes to mans body
items.note: The coverings are called the coat and cottage of Physick, and enemies to man's body.

items.quote: the Soul the Inhabitant thereof, the Super-elementall mystery the Quint-Essence, which is the true Internall, sutable, freindly and correspondent Balsom of our bodyes
items.note: What dwells within is named in a row of equal names: the Soul, the Super-elementall mystery, the Quint-Essence, the Balsom of our bodies.

items.quote: that quickning essence may be got, whose faculty mounts more high and quick being loosed from its chaines
items.note: The aim of the separating: to get the quickning essence, stronger once loosed from its chains.

items.quote: Putrefications onely are the true Correctives of all Physick.
items.note: The margin note names Putrefications alone as the true Correctives of Physick.

items.quote: As Death separateth eternall and perishing things, so doth Fire the good from the bad, the Quint-Essence from the body.
items.note: The margin note likens Fire to Death: it separates good from bad, the Quint-Essence from the body.

items.quote: Putrefications onely are the true Correctives of all Physick.
items.note: The note says Putrefications only correct Physick; CH3.20 says the poison of metals is corrected and amended by the help of this Art and of Fire, and the same note goes on to give the separating to Fire.

items.quote: All Venemous things have a Balsom agreeable to Mans Nature, and there is no poysonous Creature but hath in it an Antidote against its own poyson
items.note: Every venomous thing holds a Balsom fit for man and an antidote to its own poison.

items.quote: Spiders are good for hens and Sparrowes, Toads for Serpents, Serpents for Staggs and Storks
items.note: Examples that what is poison to man is food to another creature.

items.quote: these Formes of Physick work better when they are extracted, then whilst they are drowned in Matter, which alwayes hindereth and restraineth the power and operation of the Secret
items.note: The Formes of Physick work better extracted than left in Matter; what is extracted is also called the Secret.

items.quote: the Soule or Form of every kind of thing hath not onely more, but more excellent vertues and operations by far than either the very body, or the matter of the same thing
items.note: Soule and Form are put as one; it has more and better virtues than the body or matter of the thing.

items.quote: as every thing hath its being from the Form, by how much the more it hath of the Form, by so much the more is there of the Entity
items.note: The reason given: being comes from the Form, so more Form is more Entity.

items.quote: this the very Enemyes of Chymistry are forced to confess, being compel'd by their own conscience, and convinced thereof by ocular demonstration
items.name: the very Enemyes of Chymistry
items.note: A confession ascribed to a group, the Enemyes of Chymistry, who are said to grant the point when shown it.

items.quote: Hence many advantages follow.
items.note: The text announces a list of advantages; three numbered ones follow in CH3.17 to CH3.19.

items.quote: Reasons why the Spagyrick Physick duely prepared is to be preferd before other Hetroclite mixtures in the shops.
items.note: The margin note heads the list and names the thing preferred the Spagyrick Physick, against the Hetroclite mixtures of the shops.

items.quote: First, Because many sick people will take it more easily and willingly
items.note: First advantage: the sick take it more easily.

items.quote: those muddy and pudly potions, which spoyl the complexion of a mans body
items.note: The other medicines are called muddy potions that the prescriber himself would refuse.

items.quote: Secondly, Though these medicines be often used, yet they hurt not the stomack
items.note: Second advantage: frequent use does not hurt the stomach.

items.quote: being separate in the stomack, they are by a naturall force carryed without hinderance to their known lodgings
items.note: The reason given: being separate, they are carried by a natural force to their places, and no harsh earthy parts stay to ulcerate.

items.quote: Thirdly, Because all the hurtfull quality is altogether cast out of, or at least easily kept under in these Essences by the permixture of other most exquisite propertyes.
items.note: Third advantage: the hurtful quality is cast out, or kept under by the permixture of other properties.

items.quote: easily kept under in these Essences by the permixture of other most exquisite propertyes
items.note: Here a hurtful quality is kept under by permixture; CH3.6 says the Physitians are to seperate, not masters to compose. Whether permixture is a composing is not said in the lines given.

items.quote: this Spagyrick art is so necessary that he can be no safe Physitian who hath it not
items.note: No one is a safe Physitian without the Spagyrick art.

items.quote: many times in one simple thinge there are different substances, somtimes of contrary qualityes, whereof one may be hurtfull, the rest healthfull, as we see in Opium and honey
items.note: One simple may hold several substances of contrary qualities; Opium and honey are the examples.

items.quote: the Galenists may make good their Axioms, who affirm that all bitter things are hot
items.name: the Galenists
items.note: An axiom given to the Galenists; the author says only this Art lets them make it good, against the cases of Opium, Roses and Succory.

items.quote: The knot of this Answer must be cut with an Anatomicall knife fire
items.note: Fire is called an Anatomicall knife: the cutting is not meant of a blade.

items.quote: thus we come to understand the temperature of simples, by making a seperation of the substances
items.note: The step: separate the substances of a simple, and so learn its temperature.

items.quote: in Opium there is a sweet Narcotick Sulphur, and a bitter hot Salt penetrating by a subtile resolution and causing sweat without any stupefactive vertue
items.note: What the separation of Opium is said to yield: a sweet Narcotick Sulphur and a bitter hot Salt.

items.quote: yet may it be so corrected and amended by the help of this Art and of Fire, that it may be taken into the whole body without danger
items.note: The poison of metals can be corrected by this Art and Fire so that it is taken without danger.

items.quote: as skilfull Physitians well know, who can tell how to pick and cull the best things out of the worst
items.name: skilfull Physitians
items.note: The author calls on what skilful Physitians know as witness.

items.quote: being of an unruly malignity, yet it is tamed artificially with Salt-Peter, by the assistance of Fire
items.note: The example given: a malignant thing (its name is partly illegible in the text) is tamed with Salt-Peter and Fire.

items.quote: Poyson reduced to its Arcanum is not poyson, but a soveraign nedicine
items.note: The margin note says what poison becomes when reduced to its Arcanum: a sovereign medicine.

items.quote: stinking smells by degestion are turned into sweet savours
items.note: The margin note names degestion as what turns stinking smells sweet; it also speaks of bodies healed of a leprosy, in words partly illegible.

items.quote: Mineralls whose spirits exceed ours in subtilty, and precious stones, ought to be accounted medicinable, which rightly prepared doe much excell all Vegetables in effecting cures.
items.note: Minerals and precious stones, rightly prepared, excel all Vegetables in curing; numbered reasons follow.

items.quote: First, Because so great vertue and strong operations cannot be stampt upon such soft matter, as is that of Plants and living things
items.note: First reason: soft matter of plants and living things cannot hold so strong an impression.

items.quote: as the Spirits of perfect mettalls doe, which are not subject to corruptions
items.note: The Spirits of perfect mettalls free the body from corruption because they are not subject to it, as Vegetables are.

items.quote: there being scarce any Oyntment prepared that is not made of an imperfect mettall or minerall
items.note: Second reason: surgical ointments, nearly all made of an imperfect metal or mineral, show their virtue.

items.quote: Therefore perfect things doubtlesse have received of the Omnipotent far greater force and vertues.
items.note: Drawn from the imperfect to the perfect: perfect things have greater virtues.

items.quote: could by no means so contemper the mixture of those bodies that they should attaine to such admirable power and admit of the solid and stable Nature of a Balsom
items.note: Third reason: Nature makes living things and plants for many uses, so their mixture cannot reach the solid, stable nature of a Balsom.

items.quote: Nature therefore by length of time can adorn precious stones and other metallary bodies with a greater faculty of working
items.note: Fourth reason: the long time of generation gives stones and metallary bodies a greater faculty.

items.quote: stones require a long time of generation, but perfect bodies are generated in a shorter space
items.note: Here perfect bodies are set against stones as the quicker and lesser kind; in CH3.22 and CH3.23 perfect names the metals and things of greater virtue. The lines given do not say which bodies are meant here.

items.quote: it can hardly be spoyled or corrupted by any force of Fire, and that onely because of the fixation of spirits that may be seen in it
items.note: The Bohemian Garnat resists Fire, and the cause given is the fixation of spirits in it.

items.quote: it striveth to be as medicinable as Gold, and may well be preferd before the Orientall Rubie in Physick
items.note: The Garnat is ranked near Gold and above the Orientall Rubie for Physick, by how long each endures Fire.

items.quote: This also by the way is to be observed
items.note: The author marks what follows on the stones as an aside.

items.quote: precious stones have the Colour, Forme and Tincture more or lesse from Mettalls by formation of the Stars, for they are transplanted Mertalls
items.note: The text says what precious stones are: transplanted metals, taking colour, form and Tincture from metals.

items.quote: Gemmes are Elementary Stars.
items.note: The margin note says what Gemmes are: Elementary Stars.

items.quote: Rubies and Garnats have the Tincture of Gold, Saphirs and Turcoides of Silver, Emeralds and Chrysolites of Copper, the Jacint and Topaz of Iron
items.note: A list pairing stones with the metal whose Tincture they have.

items.quote: the Diamond of Tinne-Saturn addeth a gluish matter to the weight or heavinesse
items.note: The list goes on with the Diamond and Tinne, and with Saturn adding weight; the pointing of the sentence leaves it unclear where one statement ends and the next begins.

items.quote: those factitious and fictitious gemms that are made of the powder of red lead and white flints proportionably mixed, receiving a mettallick Forme from Fire
items.note: A concrete making: false gems from powder of red lead and white flints mixed in proportion and worked by Fire.

items.quote: the skilfull Stone-gravers can easily discerne the cheat and fraud by their softnesse and lightnesse
items.note: The made gems equal the natural in splendour but are known by softness and lightness.
